title: Choosing in order
objectives: Count ordered selections and write them with factorials.

screens.prose: Five fund managers, Ana, Ben, Cal, Dev and Eve, are up for three awards: first, second and third. Nobody can win twice.
screens.question: In how many ways can the three awards be given out?

hints.text: Who could win first place?
Fill first place, then second, then third.
5 can win first. Then 4 are left for second, then 3 for third.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the choices for first, then second, then third.

byKey.repeats: You let one manager win more than once. A winner leaves the pool, so the choices shrink.
byKey.groups: You counted the groups of three winners. Swapping who comes first gives a different result here.
byKey.added: You added 5, 4 and 3. Each award is a stage, so multiply.
byKey.all-five: You lined up all five managers. Only three places win, so stop after three factors.

explain.text: First place has 5 choices, second 4 and third 3: $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$. The other 2 managers win nothing. So the product stops after three factors.

canvas.caption: Ben, Dev, Ana is one of the 60

screens.prose: Ben has won first place and Cal second. Tap a card to select it, and tap it again to clear it.
screens.question: Tap every manager who could still win third place.

hints.text: Who has not won yet?
Ben and Cal are already on the podium.

feedback.correct: Ana, Dev and Eve: 3 managers are left for third place.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap only the managers who have not won yet.

byKey.with-winners: You tapped Ben and Cal too. They have already won, and nobody wins twice.
byKey.b: Ben has already won first place.
byKey.c: Cal has already won second place.

explain.text: Two managers are placed, so 3 are left for third. With 5 managers and 3 awards the choices run 5, 4, 3 and then stop. The 2 managers left over never get placed.

screens.prose: You filled 3 places from 5 managers, in order. An ordered choice like this is a **permutation**. We write $P(5, 3)$ for the number of ordered choices of 3 from 5, so $P(5, 3) = 60$.
screens.question: Seven managers compete for the same three awards. What is $P(7, 3)$?

hints.text: How many could win first place now?
Seven for first, six for second.
$7 \times 6 \times 5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply down from 7 for three places.

byKey.repeats: You worked out $7^3$, which lets one manager win three times.
byKey.groups: You counted the groups of three winners. The awards are ranked, so order counts.
byKey.all-seven: That is $7!$, which ranks all seven. Only three are placed.
byKey.added: You added 7, 6 and 5. The awards are stages, so they multiply.

explain.text: $P(7, 3) = 7 \times 6 \times 5 = 210$. Two more managers raised the count from 60 to 210. Each extra contender raises every factor by one.

screens.prose: Line up all 5 managers: there are $5! = 120$ orders. Only the first 3 places win. The 2 left over can stand in $2! = 2$ orders behind them.
screens.question: Which expression equals $5 \times 4 \times 3$?

options.why: You divided by the orders of the 3 places filled. Divide by the orders of the 2 left over.
You subtracted. Each podium appears $2!$ times among the $5!$ lines, so divide.
That also divides by the orders of the winners, which forgets who came first.

hints.text: In how many of the 120 full lines does Ben, Cal, Ana head the queue?
The 2 left over can follow in 2 orders.
Each podium shows up $2!$ times among the $5!$ lines. Divide.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many full lines share the same podium.

explain.text: Each podium heads exactly 2 of the 120 full lines, one for each order of the 2 left over. So $P(5, 3) = \dfrac{5!}{2!} = 60$. The bottom is the factorial of how many are left over.

screens.prose: Three places from 5 gave $\dfrac{5!}{2!}$, with 2 the number left over. Now place all 5 managers, so nobody is left over. The count must be $5! = 120$.
screens.question: The pattern gives $\dfrac{5!}{0!}$. What must $0!$ be for this to equal 120?

hints.text: What do you divide 120 by to leave 120?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the number that leaves 120 unchanged when you divide by it.

byKey.zero: Then the pattern would divide by zero, which has no value. Dividing by 1 is what leaves 120 alone.
byKey.five: That would make $\dfrac{5!}{0!} = 1$. We need the answer 120.

explain.text: Dividing 120 by $0!$ must leave 120, so $0! = 1$. It also fits the meaning: there is exactly one way to line up nobody. This is the edge case where every item is placed.

screens.prose: A desk names its trading accounts with a 4-letter code. Letters come from A to F, and no letter is used twice.
screens.question: How many codes are possible?

hints.text: How many letters could go first?
6 for the first letter, then 5 for the second.
$6 \times 5 \times 4 \times 3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply down from 6 for four places.

byKey.repeats: You let letters repeat, $6^4$. Here each letter is used at most once.
byKey.groups: You counted the sets of four letters. ABCD and DCBA are different codes.
byKey.all-six: That is $6!$, which uses all six letters. A code has only four.
byKey.added: You added 6, 5, 4 and 3. The places multiply.

explain.text: $6 \times 5 \times 4 \times 3 = 360$, which is $\dfrac{6!}{2!}$. Allowing repeats would give $6^4 = 1296$. Banning repeats removes almost three quarters of the codes.

screens.prose: A desk ranks its 2 best strategies out of 6, first and second. Kim writes $\dfrac{6!}{2!} = 360$.
screens.question: How many rankings are there?

options.why: That is Kim's answer. She divided by $2!$, the places filled. Divide by $4!$, the orders of the 4 strategies left over.
You dropped the order. First and second are different places, so swapping them gives a new ranking.
You let one strategy take both places.

hints.text: Fill the two places in turn. How many choices does each have?
6 for first, then 5 for second.
$6 \times 5 = 30$. With factorials, 4 strategies are left over: $\dfrac{6!}{4!}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the choices for first and second directly.

byKey.kim: You divided by the factorial of the places filled, as Kim did. The bottom is the factorial of the strategies left over: $4!$.

explain.text: Directly, $6 \times 5 = 30$. With factorials, 4 strategies are left over, so it is $\dfrac{6!}{4!} = \dfrac{720}{24} = 30$. Kim's $\dfrac{6!}{2!}$ is the count for 4 places, not 2.

canvas.caption: S4 first, S1 second: one of 30

screens.prose: Each time, you multiplied down from $n$ for $r$ places, then wrote it with factorials. The bottom was always the factorial of how many were left over: $$P(n, r) = n(n-1)\cdots(n-r+1) = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$$
screens.question: What is the last factor in $P(10, 4) = 10 \times 9 \times \cdots$?

options.why: You stopped at $10 - 4$. Four factors run 10, 9, 8, 7, so the last is $10 - 4 + 1$.
You ended on $r$. The product starts at $n$ and runs for $r$ factors.
That would be $10!$, which places all ten. Only four places are filled.

hints.text: Write out four factors starting from 10.
10, 9, 8, 7: four factors.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count four factors down from 10.

explain.text: Four places give four factors: $10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7$. The last is $n - r + 1 = 7$. With factorials, $\dfrac{10!}{6!}$ cancels everything from 6 down.

screens.prose: We want to show that the product of $r$ factors equals $\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: Fill the $r$ places in turn: $P(n, r) = n(n-1)\cdots(n-r+1)$.
Multiply top and bottom by $(n-r)!$, which keeps the value: $\dfrac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-r+1)\,(n-r)!}{(n-r)!}$.
The top now runs from $n$ all the way down to 1, so it is $n!$.

hints.text: Start from what you did with the cards.
The middle step adds the missing factors to the top.
Product, then multiply top and bottom by $(n-r)!$, then spot $n!$, then conclude.

feedback.correct: The missing factors turn the top into $n!$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the product, then complete the top to a factorial.

byKey.top: The top only becomes $n!$ after you multiply in $(n-r)!$. Put that step first.
byKey.times: Start from the product you counted. Then multiply top and bottom.

explain.text: You started from the product you counted. Multiplying top and bottom by $(n-r)!$ fills in the factors from $n-r$ down to 1. The top becomes $n!$, so $P(n, r) = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$.

screens.prose: A broker's app is locked with a 4-digit PIN. The firm bans repeated digits, so 1123 is not allowed but 0193 is.
screens.question: How many PINs are allowed?

hints.text: How many digits could go first?
10 for the first digit, then 9 for the second.
$10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply down from 10 for four places.

byKey.repeats: That counts every PIN, repeats included. The rule bans repeats.
byKey.groups: You counted the sets of four digits. 0193 and 3910 are different PINs.
byKey.added: You added 10, 9, 8 and 7. The places multiply.
byKey.no-zero: You started at 9, as if 0 could not come first. A PIN may start with 0.

explain.text: $10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 = 5040$, which is $\dfrac{10!}{6!}$. The rule cuts the 10,000 PINs to about half. A single random guess now succeeds 1 time in 5040, not 1 in 10,000.

ideas: An ordered choice of $r$ from $n$ multiplies $r$ factors down from $n$.
With factorials, divide $n!$ by the factorial of how many are left over.
$0! = 1$, so placing all $n$ gives $P(n, n) = n!$.

formula.name: Permutations of r from n
formula.note: Ordered choices of $r$ different items from $n$.

summary.trap: The bottom of $\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$ is the factorial of the items left over, not of the places filled.

quiz.prose: A fund allocates £50,000 to its best strategy, £30,000 to the second and £20,000 to the third. It has 10 strategies to rank.
quiz.question: In how many ways can the three allocations be made?

options.why: You dropped the order. The amounts differ, so who gets £50,000 matters.
You let one strategy take two allocations.
You added 10, 9 and 8. The places multiply.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill the three allocations in turn.

explain.text: The top allocation has 10 choices, the next 9 and the last 8. So there are $10 \times 9 \times 8 = 720$ ways.

quiz.prose: Factorials give a short way to write a product that stops early.
quiz.question: Which expression equals $9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6$?

options.why: You divided by the factorial of the 4 factors kept. Divide by the factorial of what is cut off, $5!$.
You subtracted. Cutting off factors means dividing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which factors must be cancelled from $9!$?

quiz.prose: A new exchange lists stocks under 3-letter tickers from A to Z. No letter may appear twice in a ticker.
quiz.question: How many tickers are possible?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply down from 26 for three places.

byKey.repeats: That is $26^3$, which lets letters repeat.
byKey.groups: You counted sets of three letters. ABC and CBA are different tickers.
byKey.added: You added 26, 25 and 24. The places multiply.

explain.text: $P(26, 3) = 26 \times 25 \times 24 = 15\,600$. With repeats allowed it would be $26^3 = 17\,576$.
